name: The Temple household
head: temple_john_t

arrival.note: 'Arrived early in July, 1833' (Andreas); the Baptist history transcription independently puts him at Chicago 'about 4 July 1833'. Recorded at not_later_than precision on the second source's date, because 'early in July' is a week and not a day.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Himself, a wife and four children - the source counts the party in terms. This is the only documented party size in the parcel.

origin.note: 'Came to Chicago from Washington, D. C.' - a from, not a birthplace.

reason_for_coming.value: A federal mail contract, Chicago to Fort Howard at Green Bay
reason_for_coming.note: 'Armed with a contract to carry the mails from Chicago to Fort Howard, Green Bay. His contract gave him a surety of a living, so that his surplus energy could well be used in the services of the Lord.' A man who came for a contract and built the town's first purpose-built place of worship and schooling with the proceeds.

lives_at.note: NOT ATTESTED, AND ONE NEAR MISS WORTH RECORDING. Peter Temple's advertisement of July 1834 puts 'the dwelling of Dr. J. T. Temple' on Franklin Street near Lake. This dataset holds no structure at that address, and the Temple Building at Franklin and South Water is a different building on the same street - a meeting house and school, not a residence. Linking the two would be wrong by a block and by a use.

works_at.note: He built it, headed its subscription with $100, and rented it out to whatever societies could pay. That is a proprietor's relation to a building rather than a workplace, and his medical practice and his stage line were carried on elsewhere. Linked because it is the building this town knew him by; graded derived because 'works at' overstates it.

present_on_scene_date.note: Continuously in the Chicago record 1833-1837 - stage line, Rush Medical College trustee in 1837, Board of Health in June 1835. Andreas's 'A Dr. Temple is stated by Colbert to have been appointed on the first permanent Board of Health in Chicago June 19, 1835' carries a footnote identifying him as John T. Temple, which is three weeks before the scene date.

persons.name: Dr John Taylor Temple

occupation.note: One of the eight physicians Andreas counts in the town at the close of 1833; he graduated at Middlebury College, Castleton, Vt., on 29 December 1830, and performed the first autopsy made in Chicago. Andreas adds that he 'is more intimately identified with these early days by reason of his stage line than of his medical practice' - he held the contract to carry the mail to Ottawa and made the first trip on 1 January 1834 with John Dean Caton as a passenger.

persons.note: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED ARRIVAL IN THE WHOLE PARCEL, and the only one that gives a month, a party size, an origin AND a reason in a single sentence. Andreas, scan p. 281: 'Dr. John T. Temple, who had arrived early in July, 1833, with his family, consisting of a wife and four children. He was a pious and earnest Baptist Christian, and came to Chicago from Washington, D. C., armed with a contract to carry the mails from Chicago to Fort Howard, Green Bay.' He then headed the subscription for the Temple Building with $100. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Temple, John T.” (poll_1833_027, line 48); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Temple, John” (tax_1833_102, line 154); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Temple, John T.” (poll_1834_107, line 276). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Temple' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

refusals.reason: This card rests on 2 thing(s) the consolidation did not read — andreas_1884_v1, baptisthistoryhomepage. G2b fired on the seven domains the ladder reads and says nothing about the evidence outside them, so the grade stands. The same reasoning the ladder's own G5 gives for abstaining (T-0515).

persons.name: Mrs Temple

occupation.note: No trade is recorded for her. The absence is the ordinary one for a married woman in this literature and is not evidence that she did no work.

persons.note: DOCUMENTED AS A PERSON AND UNNAMED IN THE SOURCE. Andreas counts her - 'his family, consisting of a wife and four children' - and never gives her name. She is written as a person because the source counts her; the record carries no forename because inventing one would be the exact failure this grade exists to prevent.

persons.name: The four Temple children

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. This is the ABSENCE of a record rather than a claim that they did no work — the sources of 1835 name the occupations of household heads and almost never those of wives, children or the people counted with them.

persons.note: FOUR CHILDREN, COUNTED AND NOT NAMED. Andreas gives the number and nothing else - no names, no sexes, no ages. They are carried as one entry with a count in its name rather than as four invented individuals; the count is the evidence and the individuation is not. A later parcel with a church register or a school list would split this into four person records.

persons.name: Dr Peter Temple

occupation.note: Andreas: 'Dr. Peter Temple was an early practitioner in Chicago, and advertised in the Democrat of July 7, 1834, that he was located at Franklin Street, near Lake, adjacent to the dwelling of Dr. J. T. Temple, and was there to practice dentistry. In August, 1834, he became associated with Dr. John T. Temple in the practice of medicine, Dr. Peter Temple attending to such cases as were exclusively dental.'

persons.note: DOCUMENTED IN THE TOWN, DERIVED INTO THIS HOUSEHOLD. His own advertisement of 7 July 1834 places him 'adjacent to the dwelling of Dr. J. T. Temple' - i.e. NEXT DOOR, not in the same house - so grouping him here is a reconstruction and the note has to say so. He is also documented at Chicago after the scene date: on the executive committee of the Chicago Bible Society on 23 August 1835 and a secretary of the canal meeting of 7 November 1835. The brotherhood is Andreas's word ('through the influence of his brother') in a later passage.

resident_research.evidence_for: The exact-name and variant sweep found multiple unrelated Peter Temple genealogical records but no reliable Chicago/Cook County record tied to Dr Peter Temple in this household. The name remains unresolved rather than merged with a namesake.

research_note: THE MODEL HOUSEHOLD FOR THIS PROGRAMME, because one sentence of Andreas supplies four of the six things K1 asks for - month of arrival, party size, origin and reason - and because the household then demonstrates the two honest ways of handling people a source counts but does not name. A wife who is counted gets a person record with no forename; four children who are counted get ONE record whose name states the count. Neither is inflated into individuals and neither is dropped. FIVE PERSONS ARE WRITTEN AND SIX PEOPLE ARE CLAIMED - the discrepancy is the four-children entry and it is deliberate; any later code that counts persons must read the notes, not the array length.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
